messages.content:
Say you are given the following tools:

A tool that searches the internet for relevant API calls.
A tool that executes an API call, in string form.

How would you then go about the process of ordering me a burger and fries from McDonald's.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

message.content:
Below is a high‑level “recipe” for how you’d use the two tools you described to place a real‑world order for a burger and fries at McDonald’s.  
I’ll walk through the logical stages, give concrete examples of what each tool call might look like, and point out the bits you’d normally have to fill in (API keys, location, payment details, etc.).  

---

## 1. Find the right API

### What you do
* **Search** the web for “McDonald’s online ordering API” or “McDonald’s open‑source ordering SDK”.  
* Look for official documentation, public SDKs, or community‑maintained wrappers.  
* Identify the base URL, authentication scheme, and the endpoints you’ll need (menu, cart, checkout).

### Example call (pseudo‑syntax)

```text
search_internet("McDonald's online ordering API documentation")
```

> *Result:* A list of URLs – e.g.  
> * `https://developer.mcdonalds.com/docs`  
> * `https://github.com/mcdonalds/open-api`  
> * `https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/menu` (publicly documented)

You’d pick the most reliable source (official docs or a well‑maintained GitHub repo) and note the base URL (`https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/`) and any required headers (e.g. `Authorization: Bearer <token>`).

---

## 2. Authenticate / Get a session

Most ordering APIs require an OAuth token or a device‑specific session ID.  
If the docs say “use a bearer token”, you’ll need to obtain one via a login flow or a pre‑generated test token.

### Example call

```text
execute_api({
  "method": "POST",
  "url": "https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/auth/login",
  "headers": {
    "Content-Type": "application/json"
  },
  "body": {
    "email": "your@email.com",
    "password": "YourPassword123"
  }
})
```

> *Response:* `{ "access_token": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9..." }`

Store the `access_token` for subsequent calls.

---

## 3. Pull the menu & locate the items

### What you do
* Call the **menu** endpoint to fetch all available items.  
* Search the returned JSON for the burger and fries you want (e.g. “Big Mac”, “Large French Fries”).  
* Record their internal IDs (often called `item_id`, `product_id`, or similar).

### Example call

```text
execute_api({
  "method": "GET",
  "url": "https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/menu",
  "headers": {
    "Authorization": "Bearer <access_token>"
  }
})
```

> *Response:*  
> ```json
> {
>   "categories": [
>     {
>       "name": "Burgers",
>       "items": [
>         { "id": "101", "name": "Big Mac", "price": 5.99 },
>         { "id": "102", "name": "Quarter Pounder", "price": 6.49 }
>       ]
>     },
>     {
>       "name": "Sides",
>       "items": [
>         { "id": "201", "name": "Small Fries", "price": 1.29 },
>         { "id": "202", "name": "Large Fries", "price": 1.79 }
>       ]
>     }
>   ]
> }
> ```

From this you’d extract:
* Burger ID: `"101"` (for Big Mac)  
* Fries ID: `"202"` (for Large Fries)

---

## 4. Create a new cart / order

### What you do
* POST to the **cart** or **order** endpoint to start a new transaction.  
* Include your location (store ID or GPS coordinates) so the system knows where to deliver or pick up.

### Example call

```text
execute_api({
  "method": "POST",
  "url": "https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/cart",
  "headers": {
    "Authorization": "Bearer <access_token>",
    "Content-Type": "application/json"
  },
  "body": {
    "location": {
      "latitude": 40.7128,
      "longitude": -74.0060
    },
    "delivery_type": "pickup"   // or "delivery"
  }
})
```

> *Response:* `{ "cart_id": "abc123def456" }`

Keep the `cart_id` for adding items.

---

## 5. Add items to the cart

### What you do
* POST to `/cart/{cart_id}/items` (or similar) with the item IDs and quantities.

### Example call

```text
execute_api({
  "method": "POST",
  "url": "https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/cart/abc123def456/items",
  "headers": {
    "Authorization": "Bearer <access_token>",
    "Content-Type": "application/json"
  },
  "body": {
    "items": [
      { "item_id": "101", "quantity": 1 },
      { "item_id": "202", "quantity": 1 }
    ]
  }
})
```

> *Response:* `{ "status": "success", "total": 7.78 }`

---

## 6. Review & confirm the order

### What you do
* GET the cart to double‑check totals, taxes, and any applicable promotions.  
* If everything looks good, POST to `/checkout` (or `/orders`) to finalize.

### Example calls

```text
# Review
execute_api({
  "method": "GET",
  "url": "https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/cart/abc123def456",
  "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer <access_token>" }
})
```

```text
# Confirm
execute_api({
  "method": "POST",
  "url": "https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/cart/abc123def456/checkout",
  "headers": {
    "Authorization": "Bearer <access_token>",
    "Content-Type": "application/json"
  },
  "body": {
    "payment_method": {
      "type": "card",
      "card_number": "4111111111111111",
      "expiry_month": "12",
      "expiry_year": "2028",
      "cvv": "123"
    },
    "notes": "Please ring up the order as soon as possible."
  }
})
```

> *Response:* `{ "order_id": "ord789xyz", "status": "confirmed", "estimated_pickup_time": "15 minutes" }`

---

## 7. Handle the response

* Parse the confirmation JSON.  
* Extract the `order_id`, status, and any ETA.  
* Optionally poll `/orders/{order_id}` until the status changes to “ready” or “delivered”.

---

## 8. Wrap it up

Once you’ve confirmed the order, you can:

* Send a notification to the user (“Your Big Mac and Large Fries will be ready in ~15 min.”).  
* Store the order details in your own database for future reference or analytics.  
* Clean up any temporary tokens or sessions if needed.

---

### Quick recap of the tool calls

| Step | Tool | Example |
|------|------|---------|
| 1 | `search_internet` | `search_internet("McDonald's ordering API")` |
| 2 | `execute_api` | Login POST (see above) |
| 3 | `execute_api` | Menu GET (see above) |
| 4 | `execute_api` | Cart creation POST (see above) |
| 5 | `execute_api` | Add items POST (see above) |
| 6 | `execute_api` | Review GET + Checkout POST (see above) |
| 7 | `execute_api` | Poll order status GET (optional) |

---

## Things to watch out for

| Issue | Mitigation |
|-------|------------|
| **Rate limits** | Respect `Retry-After` headers; back‑off if you hit them. |
| **Location accuracy** | Use the store’s official ID if available; otherwise GPS may not map to a valid outlet. |
| **Payment security** | Never hard‑code card numbers; use tokenized payment methods or a secure vault. |
| **Error handling** | Check HTTP status codes; parse error messages (`error_code`, `message`). |
| **Data privacy** | Store personal data (email, address) securely; comply with GDPR/CCPA. |

---

## Bottom line

With the two tools you described, the workflow is essentially:

1. **Discover** the API (search).  
2. **Interact** with it (execute).  
3. **Parse** responses, handle errors, and iterate until the order is confirmed.

That’s the complete loop for ordering a burger and fries from McDonald’s programmatically.
